words.shortDefinition: An independently deployable service built around a single business capability.
words.simpleDefinition: A microservice is a small, focused program that does one business job — like processing payments, managing inventory, or sending notifications. It runs as its own process, has its own database, and can be deployed, scaled, and restarted without touching any other part of the system.
words.longDefinition: A microservice is the fundamental unit of a microservices architecture. Each service is autonomous: it owns a specific business capability, maintains its own data store, exposes a well-defined API, and can be deployed to production independently of every other service. Teams typically align around service boundaries — one small team owns one or a few services end-to-end, from code to production monitoring. The key properties that distinguish a microservice from a module inside a monolith are: independent deployability (you can ship it without coordinating with other teams), independent scalability (you can run 20 instances of just this service), and independent failure isolation (a bug in this service does not directly crash other services). Netflix runs hundreds of microservices; each handles a distinct capability such as user authentication, content catalog, billing, or recommendation ranking.
words.connector: Think of a microservice like a specialist at a hospital — the cardiologist only handles heart issues, has their own equipment and patient records, and can take vacation without shutting down the whole hospital.
words.techContext: After extracting the order service as a microservice, the payments team could deploy billing changes three times a day without waiting for a monolith release window.
words.exampleSentence: Each microservice in our e-commerce platform owns exactly one domain — the cart service, the inventory service, and the fulfillment service deploy on completely independent schedules.
words.etymology: From Greek 'mikros' (small) + Latin 'servitium' (service). The term was popularized by Martin Fowler and James Lewis in their 2014 article defining the architectural style.

words.shortDefinition: A single deployable unit containing all application functionality.
words.simpleDefinition: A monolith is an application where all the code — the user interface, business logic, database access, and background jobs — lives in one codebase and is deployed as one unit. Changing any part requires rebuilding and redeploying the whole thing. Monoliths are a perfectly valid starting point; they become painful only when the team or the codebase grows large enough that coordinating changes becomes a bottleneck.
words.longDefinition: A monolithic application packages all functionality into a single deployable artifact. In a traditional web monolith, a single process handles HTTP requests, contains all business logic, and connects to one shared database. This design is the natural starting point for most software — it is simpler to build, test, debug, and deploy than a distributed system. Problems emerge at scale: when many teams need to deploy independently, when different parts of the application need wildly different scaling profiles, or when a bug in one module can crash the entire application. The monolith is not an anti-pattern — Stack Overflow famously served millions of daily requests with a highly optimized monolith for years. The question is whether your specific problems justify the costs of decomposition into microservices.
words.connector: Think of a monolith like a single large apartment building where all utilities — electricity, water, heat — run through one shared system. When the boiler breaks, every tenant is cold.
words.techContext: Our monolith takes 45 minutes to build and test, so a one-line bug fix blocks the entire team from shipping until the pipeline completes.
words.exampleSentence: The monolith made sense when we had three engineers, but now that we have fifteen teams all deploying from the same codebase, release coordination alone takes half a day each week.

codeExample.code:
# A monolith: all domains in one application
# users/, orders/, inventory/, billing/ — all in the same process
from flask import Flask
from users.routes import users_bp
from orders.routes import orders_bp
from inventory.routes import inventory_bp
from billing.routes import billing_bp

app = Flask(__name__)
app.register_blueprint(users_bp)
app.register_blueprint(orders_bp)
app.register_blueprint(inventory_bp)
app.register_blueprint(billing_bp)

# One deploy = all four domains deployed simultaneously
if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

words.etymology: From Greek 'monos' (single) + 'lithos' (stone) — a single solid stone, implying one indivisible block.

words.shortDefinition: The defined scope of what a service owns — its data, logic, and API surface.
words.simpleDefinition: A service boundary is the line that separates what belongs inside a service from what belongs outside it. Everything inside the boundary — data, business rules, internal implementation — is the service's private concern. Everything crossing the boundary must go through the service's public API. Drawing boundaries correctly is the hardest and most important design decision in microservices.
words.longDefinition: A service boundary defines the scope of a microservice's responsibility: what data it owns exclusively, what logic it encapsulates, and what API it exposes to the outside world. Well-drawn boundaries align with business capabilities — an order service owns everything about an order's lifecycle; an inventory service owns stock levels. Poorly drawn boundaries create coupling: if Service A must know about Service B's database schema or call seven of Service B's internal methods to do its job, the boundary is wrong. Robert C. Martin's Single Responsibility Principle applies at the service level: a service should have exactly one reason to change — one team, one business domain, one set of stakeholders. The practical signals of a wrong boundary are: services that always deploy together (merge them), services that constantly call each other in long chains (redesign the boundary), and services that require other teams to approve every change (the boundary is in the wrong place).
words.connector: Think of a service boundary like property lines between houses — you own what's inside your fence, you mow your own lawn, and your neighbor can't come dig up your garden without asking.
words.techContext: We realized our user-service boundary was wrong when we discovered the cart service was directly querying the users table to get shipping addresses — the address data belonged inside user-service's boundary.
words.exampleSentence: After redrawing the service boundary to move address management into the user service, the cart service dropped from five internal dependencies to one clean API call.
words.etymology: Compound of 'service' (Latin 'servitium') + 'boundary' (Old French 'bodne', limit). Popularized in software by Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design (2003) and refined for microservices by Sam Newman in 'Building Microservices' (2015) as the primary unit of system decomposition.

words.shortDefinition: Application Programming Interface — the contract a service exposes to callers.
words.simpleDefinition: An API is the set of operations a service makes available to the outside world — the buttons and levers other services or applications can press to interact with it. In microservices, an API is the only legitimate way to ask another service for data or to trigger an action. Everything else (direct database access, shared memory) is a violation of the service boundary.
words.longDefinition: In a microservices context, an API is the formal interface through which a service communicates with the world. It is the published contract: here are the operations you can call, here are the expected inputs, here are the possible outputs. The API is intentionally the only channel through which a service's capabilities are accessible — it hides all internal implementation details. This encapsulation is what makes independent deployability possible: as long as the API contract does not break, the service's internals can be rewritten entirely without consumers noticing. APIs in microservices are most commonly HTTP/REST, gRPC, or asynchronous message contracts. The API surface should be the smallest that satisfies consumers — exposing too much creates coupling; exposing too little forces workarounds that bypass the boundary.
words.connector: Think of an API like the menu at a restaurant — it tells you what you can order, what you need to specify ("medium rare"), and what you'll get back. You don't need to know how the kitchen works.
words.techContext: When we refactored the order service's internal data model, we froze the public API surface and all twelve downstream consumers continued working without any changes.
words.exampleSentence: The payments team owns the payments API contract; no other service reads the payments database directly — all integrations go through the API.

codeExample.code:
# OpenAPI snippet — the contract a service publishes
openapi: "3.0.3"
info:
  title: Inventory Service API
  version: "1.0"
paths:
  /inventory/{sku}:
    get:
      summary: Get available stock for a SKU
      parameters:
        - name: sku
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: { type: string }
      responses:
        "200":
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                properties:
                  sku: { type: string }
                  available: { type: integer }

words.etymology: Acronym for Application Programming Interface; coined in the early days of computing to describe the interface through which programs invoke operating system or library functions.

words.shortDefinition: A design quality where all elements within a service belong together — every operation serves the same business responsibility.
words.simpleDefinition: High cohesion means that everything inside a service is closely related and works toward the same purpose. An order service that handles order creation, order updates, and order queries is highly cohesive — all its code serves one business responsibility. A service that also sends emails, resizes images, and calculates inventory is low-cohesion: unrelated concerns are bundled together and will pull the service in different directions as the product evolves.
words.longDefinition: Cohesion measures how strongly related the responsibilities inside a module or service are. In microservices, high cohesion is the design goal: every endpoint, every data model, every piece of business logic in a service should be there because it belongs to the same business capability. Robert C. Martin's Single Responsibility Principle applied at the service level states that a service should have one reason to change — meaning one business stakeholder drives its evolution. High cohesion and loose coupling are complementary: cohesion is about what stays together (the things a service owns), coupling is about what stays apart (the dependencies between services). A highly cohesive service is easier to understand (all its code relates to one domain), easier to test (one domain's rules to cover), and easier to deploy (one team's decisions drive its changes). Low-cohesion services become bottlenecks: multiple teams need to change them for unrelated reasons, so they become coordination hotspots and sources of instability.
words.connector: Think of high cohesion like a toolbox organized by craft — all the carpentry tools are together, all the plumbing tools are together. A box with one hammer, one wrench, one paint brush, and one soldering iron is low-cohesion: it serves no single purpose well.
words.techContext: When we split our 'utility service' into three cohesive services — notification, file-storage, and currency-conversion — each team's deployment rate tripled because they no longer shared a release cycle.
words.exampleSentence: The shipping service exhibits high cohesion: every endpoint, model, and rule inside it exists solely to manage the lifecycle of a physical shipment — no billing logic, no user management, no email sending.
words.etymology: From Latin 'cohaesio' (a sticking together), from 'cohaerere' (to cling together). In software engineering, the concept was formalized by Larry Constantine and Edward Yourdon in 'Structured Design' (1979), which introduced a scale from coincidental cohesion (lowest) to functional cohesion (highest).

words.shortDefinition: The decision of how much business responsibility to pack into one service — too small creates nanoservices, too large recreates the monolith.
words.simpleDefinition: Service granularity is about finding the right size for a microservice. Make a service too large and you recreate the monolith — everything coupled together, slow to change. Make it too small and you get nanoservices — each service does one trivial thing, and every operation requires ten network calls to complete. The right size is the one where a small team can own, understand, and deploy the service independently, and where the business capability it serves is clear and stable.
words.longDefinition: Service granularity is one of the central design decisions in microservices architecture and one of the hardest to get right. Granularity is often described in terms of cohesion and coupling: a service should be fine-grained enough to be highly cohesive (every line of code relates to one business capability) but coarse-grained enough that it rarely needs to call out to other services to complete a single operation. The nanoservice anti-pattern (term attributed to Arnon Rotem-Gal-Oz) occurs when services are split too finely — each network call, authentication check, or validation step becomes its own service. The operational overhead is immense and latency explodes. The correct granularity signal is alignment with a team's cognitive ownership: a service is the right size when one team can understand it completely, evolve it independently, and deploy it on their own schedule without coordinating with other teams. Sam Newman's rule of thumb: start coarser than you think you need and split only when a real pain point (too many simultaneous code changes, too many teams touching the same service) emerges.
words.connector: Think of service granularity like cutting a cake — too thick and each slice is unwieldy, too thin and the slices crumble and fall apart. The right cut is the one where each portion is self-contained and manageable.
words.techContext: Our initial decomposition split the user domain into twelve services — authentication, profile, preferences, avatar, address, billing address, and six more. Latency exploded. We merged them back to three coarser services aligned with team ownership.
words.exampleSentence: We settled on order-service granularity at the full order lifecycle rather than splitting into create-order-service and fulfill-order-service — the coordination cost of two services outweighed the independence benefit.

codeExample.code:
# Service granularity spectrum — too fine vs. appropriate

# TOO FINE (nanoservices anti-pattern)
services:
  - name: validate-email-service     # one function per service
  - name: hash-password-service      # trivial, high latency overhead
  - name: check-username-service
  - name: store-user-service
  # A single user registration requires 4 network calls

# APPROPRIATE granularity
services:
  - name: identity-service           # owns auth, registration, password
  - name: profile-service            # owns display name, avatar, prefs
  - name: billing-service            # owns payment methods, invoices
  # A single user registration = 1 call, single team owner

words.etymology: From Latin 'granulum' (small grain), via 'granular' (consisting of fine particles). In software architecture, 'granularity' emerged in the 1990s object-oriented design literature to describe the size and scope of components; adopted into microservices vocabulary from Sam Newman's 'Building Microservices' (2015).

words.shortDefinition: A specific URL path a service exposes to handle a type of request.
words.simpleDefinition: An endpoint is a specific address within a service's API that handles one type of operation. For example, a user service might have an endpoint at /users/{id} that returns user data when called with GET, and an endpoint at /users that creates a new user when called with POST. Each endpoint is a named, callable point of entry into the service.
words.longDefinition: In a microservices REST API, an endpoint is the combination of an HTTP method and a URL path that maps to a specific handler in the service. Endpoints are the individual operations that make up a service's API contract. A well-designed service has a minimal set of endpoints that expose its capabilities without leaking internal implementation details. Each endpoint should have a clear purpose, predictable inputs and outputs, and documented error responses. In gRPC services, the equivalent concept is a method defined in the protobuf service definition. The sum of all a service's endpoints constitutes its API surface — the larger the surface, the more coupling opportunities and the harder the service is to evolve without breaking consumers.
words.connector: Think of endpoints like doors into a building — each door leads to a different room for a different purpose, and you can only enter through labeled entrances rather than punching holes in the walls.
words.techContext: We audited the payment service's endpoints and found six that were called by exactly zero consumers — removing them shrank the API contract and reduced the surface we had to maintain.
words.exampleSentence: The fulfillment service exposes three endpoints: one to query shipment status, one to create a shipment, and one to trigger a return — each maps to exactly one business operation.
words.etymology: Compound of 'end' (terminus) + 'point' (location). In networking, an endpoint originally referred to either end of a communication channel; in web APIs it evolved to mean a specific addressable operation.

words.shortDefinition: A message sent from a caller to a service asking it to perform an action or return data.
words.simpleDefinition: A request is the message a client sends to a service to ask it to do something — retrieve data, create a resource, trigger a workflow. In HTTP-based microservices, a request consists of a method (GET, POST, etc.), a URL, headers describing the request context, and optionally a body with the data being sent. The service receives the request, processes it, and sends back a response.
words.longDefinition: In the request-response communication model that underlies synchronous microservice interactions, a request is the initiating message. It carries all the information the service needs to process the operation: the target resource (URL), the intended action (HTTP method), authorization credentials (headers), content negotiation preferences, and the payload (body). A well-formed request is self-describing — the server needs no prior context or session state to handle it. This is REST's statelessness constraint in practice. In microservices, requests cross a network boundary, so they carry latency, can be dropped or retried, and can be intercepted or inspected by observability tooling. Every synchronous call between services is a request-response pair, and the latency budget of a user-facing operation is the sum of all request round trips in its call chain.
words.connector: Think of a request like a form you hand to a bank teller — it spells out exactly what you want done, includes your identification, and the teller processes it and hands back a reply slip.
words.techContext: Tracing the slow checkout path revealed that processing a single user request triggered 12 downstream service requests, each adding 30-80ms of latency before the user saw a confirmation.
words.exampleSentence: Every request to the pricing service includes a customer segment header so the service can apply the correct discount tier without a separate lookup.

codeExample.code:
# An HTTP request with all its components
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/orders \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGc...' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'X-Request-ID: req-550e8400' \
  -d '{
    "customerId": "cust-42",
    "items": [{"sku": "WID-001", "qty": 1}]
  }'
# Method: POST  URL: /orders  Headers: auth + content-type
# Body: the data being sent along with the request

words.etymology: From Latin 'requestus', past participle of 'requirere' (to require, ask for). In computing, usage emerged with early networking protocols to describe the initiating message in a client-server exchange.

words.shortDefinition: The message a service sends back to a caller after processing a request.
words.simpleDefinition: A response is what a service sends back after it receives and processes a request. In HTTP, a response includes a status code (200 for success, 404 for not found, 500 for server error), headers with metadata, and usually a body with the result. The status code is the primary signal about whether the request succeeded, failed, or needs the caller to take further action.
words.longDefinition: In HTTP-based microservice communication, a response is the server's reply to a client request. It carries three key pieces of information: a status code (a three-digit number indicating the outcome), response headers (metadata like Content-Type, caching instructions, rate limit counters), and an optional body (the result data). Status codes follow a standard taxonomy: 2xx (success), 3xx (redirection), 4xx (client error — the request was malformed), 5xx (server error — the service failed). Designing consistent, meaningful responses is part of the API contract: consumers depend on the status codes to handle errors correctly, on the response shape to parse the data, and on error response bodies to display useful messages. In distributed systems, responses can arrive late, out of order (in async systems), or not at all — designing for partial failure means never assuming a missing response means success.
words.connector: Think of a response like a letter back from a government agency — it starts with a code indicating the outcome (approved, denied, missing information), followed by the official explanation and any data you requested.
words.techContext: We standardized all error responses across our microservices to include a machine-readable error code, a human message, and a request-id — which cut debugging time in half.
words.exampleSentence: The inventory service returns a 409 Conflict response when a reservation request exceeds available stock, so the caller can display an appropriate out-of-stock message rather than silently failing.
words.etymology: From Latin 'responsus', past participle of 'respondere' (to answer). In HTTP, the response is formally defined in RFC 7230 as the message sent by a server after receiving and parsing a request.

words.shortDefinition: A request pattern where each call carries all needed context — the server stores no session between requests.
words.simpleDefinition: A stateless service treats each incoming request as completely independent. The service does not remember anything about previous calls from the same client. All the information needed to process the request — who you are, what you want, what parameters apply — must be included in the request itself. This means any instance of the service can handle any request, which makes horizontal scaling straightforward.
words.longDefinition: Statelessness is one of REST's foundational constraints and a core property of well-designed microservices. A stateless service holds no client-specific session state between requests. Every request must be fully self-describing: it carries its own authentication token (JWT, API key), all necessary parameters, and any context the server needs to process it. Because no instance holds session-specific data, a load balancer can route requests to any running instance. Scaling out is as simple as starting more instances — they are all equivalent. Stateless services also restart cleanly: a crash loses no user data because nothing was stored in the process. The trade-off is slightly larger requests (you carry your authentication token on every call) and the inability to hold server-side session objects — but those costs are dwarfed by the operational benefits at scale.
words.connector: Think of a stateless service like a vending machine — it doesn't remember you from your last visit; you put in your coins and make your selection fresh every time, and any machine in the building will serve you equally.
words.techContext: Because our API services are stateless and store no session data, we can scale from 3 to 50 instances under load without any session affinity configuration or data migration.
words.exampleSentence: The stateless design of the recommendation service means we can add or remove instances instantly during traffic spikes without worrying about sticky sessions or state rehydration.

codeExample.code:
# Stateless: all context comes from the request itself
from fastapi import FastAPI, Header
from jose import jwt

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/recommendations")
async def get_recommendations(
    authorization: str = Header(...),  # auth token in every request
    user_segment: str = Header(...)    # context in every request
):
    # No session lookup — decode everything from the request
    claims = jwt.decode(authorization.split()[1], SECRET)
    user_id = claims["sub"]
    # Any instance can serve this — no affinity needed
    return recommend_for(user_id, user_segment)

words.etymology: Compound of 'state' (condition, data at a point in time) + '-less' (without). In computing, the term describes protocols and services that do not maintain state across interactions.

words.shortDefinition: A service that stores session or conversational context between calls from the same client.
words.simpleDefinition: A stateful service remembers information about a client between requests — a shopping cart in progress, a multi-step checkout flow, or a WebSocket connection's state. Because the state is tied to a specific server instance, the client must keep talking to the same instance (sticky sessions), or the state must be stored somewhere shared (a Redis cache, a database) so any instance can access it.
words.longDefinition: A stateful service maintains data about a specific client's session across multiple requests. Unlike stateless services where any instance is interchangeable, a stateful service requires that subsequent requests from the same client reach either the same instance (sticky sessions via load balancer affinity) or that state is externalized to a shared store so any instance can pick it up. Stateful services are harder to scale: adding instances doesn't help unless state is distributed, and crashing an instance can lose in-flight session data. In microservices architecture, the goal is to push statefulness into dedicated storage tiers (databases, caches, message queues) and keep the service layer stateless. However, some problems genuinely require stateful services — WebSocket connections, streaming sessions, long-running workflow engines, or gaming servers that need sub-millisecond access to shared state.
words.connector: Think of a stateful service like a personal trainer who remembers your fitness history and picks up the workout exactly where you left off last session — but if they quit, you have to start over with a new trainer.
words.techContext: Our game session service is stateful — it holds the live game state in memory for sub-millisecond access — so we use sticky load balancing and take rolling snapshots to Redis every five seconds to survive instance failures.
words.exampleSentence: The checkout wizard is stateful, maintaining progress through a five-step flow in a Redis-backed session so any service instance can resume it if the original instance restarts.

codeExample.code:
# Stateful: session state stored externally so any instance can access it
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host="session-store", decode_responses=True)

@app.post("/checkout/step/{step}")
async def checkout_step(session_id: str, step: int, data: dict):
    # Load existing session state from shared Redis
    session = r.hgetall(f"checkout:{session_id}")
    session.update(data)
    session["current_step"] = step
    # Save back — any instance can serve the next request
    r.hset(f"checkout:{session_id}", mapping=session)
    r.expire(f"checkout:{session_id}", 3600)  # 1-hour TTL
    return {"step": step, "complete": step == 5}

words.etymology: Compound of 'state' + '-ful' (full of, characterized by). Contrasts with 'stateless'; the terms became prominent in distributed systems literature in the 1990s.

words.shortDefinition: The property where repeating an operation produces the same result as doing it once.
words.simpleDefinition: An idempotent operation can be safely retried any number of times without causing unintended side effects. Charging a credit card is not idempotent — running it twice charges twice. Updating a record's status to 'confirmed' is idempotent — doing it three times still results in 'confirmed'. In microservices, network failures cause retries, so operations that mutate state must be designed for idempotency to avoid double-charging, double-booking, or duplicate processing.
words.longDefinition: Idempotency is a mathematical property borrowed into distributed systems engineering: applying the same operation multiple times produces the same result as applying it once. In microservices, networks are unreliable — a request might be sent, the server might process it successfully, but the response gets lost. The caller does not know whether the operation succeeded, so it retries. If the operation is not idempotent, this retry causes a duplicate effect. The canonical dangerous example is payment processing: a network timeout after the charge succeeds but before the response arrives causes the client to retry, resulting in a double charge. Solutions include idempotency keys (the client sends a unique request ID; the server records it and returns the cached result on retries), natural idempotency by design (PUT to a specific URL is inherently idempotent — it sets the resource to the given state regardless of how many times you call it), and conditional writes (only update if the current state matches expected).
words.connector: Think of idempotency like pressing an elevator button — pressing it five times doesn't call five elevators, it just makes sure the elevator is coming. The outcome is the same no matter how many times you press.
words.techContext: After adding idempotency key support to the payment endpoint, our retry logic finally became safe — duplicate network retries during outages stopped causing double charges.
words.exampleSentence: We added an idempotency key to every payment request so that if the mobile app retries after a timeout, the charge happens exactly once regardless of how many retry attempts the network triggers.

codeExample.code:
import hashlib

@app.post("/payments")
async def charge_card(request: PaymentRequest,
                     idempotency_key: str = Header(...)):
    # Check if we've already processed this exact request
    cached = await redis.get(f"idem:{idempotency_key}")
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)  # Return the original response

    # Process the charge only if this is the first attempt
    result = await payment_gateway.charge(
        amount=request.amount,
        card_token=request.card_token
    )

    # Store result so retries get the same answer
    await redis.setex(f"idem:{idempotency_key}", 86400, json.dumps(result))
    return result

words.etymology: From Latin 'idem' (the same) + 'potens' (powerful, having an effect). Mathematical usage dates to 19th-century algebra; adopted in computing in the 1960s via HTTP specification and distributed systems research.

words.shortDefinition: Strategies (URI path, header, query param) for evolving an API without breaking existing consumers.
words.simpleDefinition: API versioning lets you make breaking changes to an API while keeping existing clients working. Instead of forcing every consumer to update simultaneously, you run two versions in parallel. Common approaches: include the version in the URL (/v1/orders vs /v2/orders), pass it in a header (Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2), or use a query parameter (?version=2). Consumers migrate to the new version on their own schedule.
words.longDefinition: In a microservices system, a service's API is a shared contract with potentially dozens of consumers. When a service needs to change its API in a breaking way — removing a field, renaming a resource, changing a required parameter — it cannot simply make the change and redeploy. That would instantly break all consumers. API versioning provides a migration path: the old and new API versions coexist, consumers migrate at their own pace, and the old version is deprecated and removed only after all consumers have migrated. Three common strategies: URI versioning (version in the path: /v1/orders, /v2/orders) is visible and easy to route but couples the version into the client's URL construction; header versioning (Accept or custom header: X-API-Version: 2) keeps URLs clean but is less discoverable; query parameter versioning (?version=2) is easy to test in a browser but considered less RESTful. Regardless of strategy, the key discipline is maintaining a deprecation timeline and communicating it to consumers.
words.connector: Think of API versioning like publishing a software manual in multiple editions — the second edition is available, but the first edition stays in print until everyone has switched over, so nobody's workflow breaks mid-sentence.
words.techContext: When we redesigned the user profile API to separate shipping addresses into their own resource, we ran v1 and v2 in parallel for six months with a deprecation notice, giving all fourteen consumer teams time to migrate.
words.exampleSentence: The payment service runs both v1 and v2 endpoints simultaneously — the iOS app migrated to v2's improved error schema last quarter, while the legacy desktop client still uses v1 until their Q3 release.
words.etymology: Compound of 'API' + 'versioning' (the practice of assigning and managing version identifiers). Became essential practice as microservices created many independent API consumers that could not coordinate upgrades.

words.shortDefinition: The rule that each microservice exclusively owns its own data store and no other service reads it directly.
words.simpleDefinition: Database per service means each microservice has its own private database that no other service is allowed to access directly. If Service B needs data that lives in Service A's database, it must call Service A's API — it cannot run a query against Service A's database tables. This rule is what makes services truly independent: you can change your database schema, switch database technologies, or restructure your data without asking anyone else's permission.
words.longDefinition: Database per service is the foundational data management pattern in microservices architecture. It means each service has its own data store — its own schema, its own tables or collections, its own connection pool — and no other service may directly read from or write to it. Data flows between services only through APIs or published events. This isolation delivers several key benefits: schema freedom (a service can refactor its internal data model without coordinating with consumers), technology choice (each service picks the storage technology best suited to its data — relational for transactions, document store for flexible schemas, graph for relationships), and independent scaling (the service with the highest data volume scales its database independently). The cost is that distributed transactions — operations that must atomically span multiple services' databases — become impossible without saga patterns or eventual consistency. Chris Richardson identifies shared databases as the most common cause of distributed monoliths in practice.
words.connector: Think of database per service like each department having its own filing cabinet that only they can access — if Finance needs information from HR, they have to ask HR to look it up for them, rather than rifling through HR's files directly.
words.techContext: The shared database anti-pattern caught up with us when the inventory team tried to add a new column — they discovered four other services were directly querying inventory tables and would break without coordinated changes.
words.exampleSentence: With database per service enforced, the catalog team migrated from PostgreSQL to MongoDB last quarter without filing a single change request with other teams — the API contract stayed the same.

codeExample.code:
# Each service has its own DB credentials and schema
# Order service — only talks to orders_db
order-service:
  environment:
    DATABASE_URL: postgres://orders_db:5432/orders

# Inventory service — only talks to inventory_db
inventory-service:
  environment:
    DATABASE_URL: postgres://inventory_db:5432/inventory

# If order service needs inventory data, it calls the API:
# GET https://inventory-service/inventory/{sku}
# NOT: SELECT * FROM inventory_db.inventory WHERE sku = ?

words.etymology: Pattern name coined by Chris Richardson in 'Microservices Patterns' (2018). The concept formalizes data encapsulation at the service level, extending object-oriented data hiding principles to distributed systems.

words.shortDefinition: The formal public boundary a service exposes to its consumers — methods, data shapes, and behavioral guarantees.
words.simpleDefinition: A service interface is the public face of a microservice — everything a consumer needs to know to call it and nothing more. It specifies what operations the service supports, what data to send in, what data comes back, and what errors can occur. Internal implementation details — databases, algorithms, helper functions — stay hidden. The interface is the contract that consumers depend on; the internals are free to change without affecting anyone outside.
words.longDefinition: A service interface is the formal boundary that separates a service's public contract from its private implementation. Well-designed service interfaces have three properties: completeness (everything a consumer legitimately needs is accessible), encapsulation (no internal details leak through the surface), and stability (the interface changes rarely and only in backward-compatible ways). In REST APIs, the service interface is expressed as an OpenAPI specification — paths, HTTP methods, request schemas, response schemas, error codes. In gRPC services, it is the .proto service definition. In event-driven systems, the service interface includes the events it publishes and their schemas. The discipline of interface design is fundamental to achieving independent deployability: as long as the interface is stable, the team behind the service can refactor internals freely. Breaking interface changes must be versioned (v1, v2) and the old version maintained until all consumers migrate. The service interface is what distinguishes a microservice from a library — a library is linked into the caller, an interface is a network boundary the caller cannot cross.
words.connector: Think of a service interface like a restaurant menu — it tells you exactly what you can order, what to expect, and what it costs. What happens in the kitchen is hidden. The menu can stay the same even if the chef changes the recipe.
words.techContext: When we documented the inventory service interface with OpenAPI and generated client SDKs from it, integration time for new consumers dropped from days to hours — the interface was the single source of truth.
words.exampleSentence: The payment service interface exposes three operations — authorize, capture, and refund — with precise schemas for each; the underlying gateway integrations can be swapped without any consumer knowing.

codeExample.code:
# Service interface expressed as OpenAPI
openapi: "3.0.3"
info:
  title: Payment Service Interface
  version: "2.0"
paths:
  /payments/authorize:
    post:
      summary: Reserve funds without capturing
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              required: [orderId, amount, currency, paymentMethodId]
              properties:
                orderId:         { type: string }
                amount:          { type: number }
                currency:        { type: string, pattern: '^[A-Z]{3}$' }
                paymentMethodId: { type: string }
      responses:
        "200": { description: Authorization reference returned }
        "402": { description: Insufficient funds }
        "422": { description: Invalid payment method }

words.etymology: Compound of 'service' (Latin 'servitium', duty or work done for another) + 'interface' (Latin 'inter', between + 'facies', face or surface). In computing, 'interface' gained its technical meaning through object-oriented programming; in distributed systems it describes the network-accessible boundary of a service.

words.shortDefinition: The ability to ship one service to production without coordinating with or redeploying other services.
words.simpleDefinition: Independent deployability means you can deploy changes to one service without any other service needing to change, redeploy, or even restart. It is the primary practical benefit of microservices over monoliths: the payments team can ship a billing change on Tuesday afternoon without waiting for the search team's Friday release window. This is only possible if services communicate through stable API contracts and don't share databases.
words.longDefinition: Independent deployability is the defining property that separates microservices from a distributed monolith. A service is independently deployable when changes to it — bug fixes, new features, performance improvements — can be pushed to production without coordinating a simultaneous release with any other service. This requires: a stable API contract that backward-compatible changes do not break, the database-per-service pattern (so schema changes only affect one team), no shared mutable state, and feature flags for changes that need to be toggled without redeployment. Independent deployability is not just a technical property — it is an organizational one. It is what lets teams operate autonomously, move at different speeds, and take responsibility for their own reliability. Sam Newman and the Google DORA research both identify independent deployability as the single most impactful capability for software delivery performance.
words.connector: Think of independent deployability like a food court where each stall operates completely on its own schedule — the sushi counter can renovate its counter on a Tuesday without closing the pizza stall next door.
words.techContext: Once we eliminated the shared sessions database, the auth service became independently deployable — previously, any auth change required a coordinated release with six downstream services that read session state directly.
words.exampleSentence: Independent deployability was our first milestone: we knew we'd achieved microservices architecture on the day our checkout team deployed a change to production without sending a single Slack message to any other team.
words.etymology: Compound of 'independent' (Latin 'independens' — not hanging from) + 'deployability' (from French 'déployer', to unfold or spread out). Established as a formal criterion for microservices by Sam Newman ('Building Microservices', 2015) and validated as a key elite-performer trait in the DORA State of DevOps research.

words.shortDefinition: The caller sends a request and waits, blocking until the response arrives.
words.simpleDefinition: Synchronous communication is the call-and-wait model. Service A calls Service B and holds a connection open, doing nothing until Service B replies. It is the familiar model of function calls — simple to reason about, easy to debug, and natural for operations where the caller genuinely needs the answer before it can proceed. The cost is that if Service B is slow or down, Service A is stuck waiting.
words.longDefinition: In synchronous communication, the caller blocks — suspends its current execution — until the callee returns a response. In HTTP microservices, this means the calling service holds an open TCP connection and waits. Synchronous communication is the default model for request/response HTTP calls and gRPC unary calls. Its primary strength is simplicity: the execution flow is linear and easy to trace, errors are immediately propagated to the caller, and debugging a failure is straightforward. Its systemic weakness in microservices is temporal coupling: the caller's availability is directly linked to the callee's. A 5xx response or timeout in Service B immediately degrades Service A. In a chain of five synchronous calls, the system's effective availability is the product of each service's individual availability (e.g., 99.9%^5 ≈ 99.5%). Mitigation patterns — circuit breakers, timeouts, bulkheads — address the coupling problem at the cost of added complexity.
words.connector: Think of synchronous communication like a phone call — you dial, wait for someone to answer, have the conversation, and only hang up when you're done. If the other person doesn't pick up, you're stuck on hold.
words.techContext: Our checkout flow makes five synchronous calls — inventory, pricing, promotion, tax, and fraud scoring — each with a 200ms budget. When fraud scoring started timing out at 350ms, checkout latency spiked and conversion dropped.
words.exampleSentence: Synchronous communication between the cart and pricing service means every cart page load waits for a live pricing response — we added aggressive caching after the pricing service's P95 latency hit 800ms.

codeExample.code:
import httpx

async def get_checkout_total(cart_id: str) -> dict:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=2.0) as client:
        # Synchronous: we wait for each response before proceeding
        cart     = await client.get(f"/carts/{cart_id}")       # wait
        pricing  = await client.post("/pricing", json=cart.json())  # wait
        tax      = await client.post("/tax", json=pricing.json())  # wait
    # Only reaches here after ALL three services have responded
    return {"cart": cart_id, "total": tax.json()["total"]}

words.etymology: From Greek 'syn' (together) + 'chronos' (time) — occurring at the same time. In computing, synchronous operations proceed in lock-step: the next instruction waits for the current one to complete.

words.shortDefinition: The caller sends a message and immediately continues — the receiver processes it later.
words.simpleDefinition: Asynchronous communication means the sender fires off a message and immediately moves on without waiting for a reply. The receiver picks up and processes the message at its own pace. This breaks the tight dependency between sender and receiver: even if the receiving service is temporarily down, the messages pile up in a queue or topic and get processed when it recovers. The trade-off is that you lose the immediate feedback of knowing whether the operation succeeded.
words.longDefinition: Asynchronous communication decouples services in time. The producing service publishes a message — an event or a command — to a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) and returns immediately. The consuming service processes the message independently, at its own pace, potentially much later. This temporal decoupling eliminates the cascading failure problem of synchronous calls: if the consuming service is slow or temporarily down, messages accumulate in the broker and drain when the service recovers. The producer is unaffected. Async communication is the natural model for event-driven architectures and the backbone of most high-throughput microservices systems. The challenges: you lose immediate error feedback (the producer does not know if processing succeeded), you must design consumers to be idempotent (messages may be delivered more than once), and debugging failures requires correlating events across services, which demands distributed tracing and careful logging.
words.connector: Think of asynchronous communication like dropping a letter in a mailbox — you post it and walk away. The recipient reads and responds whenever they get to it, and the mail system handles delivery even if the recipient is on vacation.
words.techContext: Switching order completion from a synchronous call to an async event on Kafka cut our checkout response time from 1.8 seconds to 340ms and eliminated the blast radius when the fulfillment service had outages.
words.exampleSentence: Order placement publishes an OrderCreated event asynchronously — inventory, shipping, and billing all consume it independently, so a billing outage never blocks a customer from placing an order.

codeExample.code:
from aiokafka import AIOKafkaProducer
import json

async def place_order(order: Order) -> dict:
    # 1. Write to our own database (synchronous, within our service)
    order_id = await db.insert_order(order)

    # 2. Publish event and immediately return — do NOT wait for consumers
    producer = AIOKafkaProducer(bootstrap_servers="kafka:9092")
    await producer.start()
    event = {"type": "OrderPlaced", "orderId": order_id, **order.dict()}
    await producer.send("order-events", json.dumps(event).encode())
    await producer.stop()

    # Return immediately — inventory/fulfillment/billing react in their own time
    return {"orderId": order_id, "status": "accepted"}

words.etymology: From Greek 'a-' (not) + 'syn' (together) + 'chronos' (time) — not occurring at the same time. Widely adopted in computing to describe non-blocking, deferred execution models.

words.shortDefinition: An immutable record that something happened in a service, published for other services to consume.
words.simpleDefinition: An event is a message that says something has already happened — not a request for something to happen. Events are past-tense facts: OrderPlaced, PaymentProcessed, UserRegistered. The service that emits an event does not care who reacts to it or when. Any number of other services can subscribe and take independent actions. This makes the system extensible: you can add a new service that reacts to existing events without touching the event producer.
words.longDefinition: An event is an immutable, past-tense record of a significant state change within a service. Events are the fundamental unit of asynchronous communication in event-driven microservices architectures. Key properties: events describe facts (something that already happened), not commands (something to do); they are immutable (you cannot un-fire an event); and they are typically published to a durable broker where they can be replayed. The naming convention matters: OrderPlaced is an event; PlaceOrder is a command. An event producer publishes without knowing (or caring) which consumers exist. This one-to-many, fire-and-forget model is what enables extensibility — a new analytics service, a new fraud detection service, or a new notification service can begin consuming existing events without any change to the producing service. Events are the backbone of event-driven architecture, saga choreography, and event sourcing patterns.
words.connector: Think of an event like a newspaper headline — it records what happened, is published for anyone to read, and is true whether or not anyone reads it. Adding new readers doesn't require notifying the newspaper.
words.techContext: When we needed to add real-time fraud scoring to checkout, we subscribed to the existing OrderPlaced event instead of changing the order service — the order service never knew the fraud service existed.
words.exampleSentence: Every state change in the order lifecycle publishes an event — OrderPlaced, OrderConfirmed, OrderShipped, OrderDelivered — and any service that needs to react to order changes subscribes independently.
words.etymology: From Latin 'eventus' (outcome, result), from 'evenire' (to come out, happen). In distributed systems, usage was formalized in the event-driven architecture literature of the 1980s and 1990s.

words.shortDefinition: Incrementally migrating a monolith by building new services alongside it and routing traffic away until the monolith can be removed.
words.simpleDefinition: The strangler fig pattern is the safe way to migrate from a monolith to microservices. Instead of a risky big-bang rewrite, you pick one capability at a time, build a new service for it, use a proxy to route that capability's traffic to the new service, and delete the old code from the monolith. Production always works. You can reverse any step. The monolith gradually shrinks as the new services grow around it — until eventually you can switch off the monolith entirely.
words.longDefinition: Named by Martin Fowler after the strangler fig tree (Ficus aurea), which wraps around a host tree, gradually taking its resources and eventually replacing it — the host tree dies but the strangler fig stands. Applied to software: a new system grows incrementally around the existing monolith, redirecting traffic capability by capability until the monolith can be decommissioned. The migration proceeds in three repeating steps: identify a capability to extract (ideally one with a clean interface that changes frequently), build the new service alongside the running monolith, then route traffic for that capability through an API gateway or proxy to the new service. Each extraction is independently reversible. Production is never in a broken state. This contrasts with the rewrite anti-pattern — spending 18 months building a replacement in secret and performing a big-bang cutover that is extremely difficult to roll back. Shopify's migration from its Rails monolith, and the many migrations at Amazon, Netflix, and Uber from early monoliths all used strangler fig approaches.
words.connector: Think of the strangler fig pattern like a renovation where you move room by room rather than demolishing the whole house — you live in it throughout, each room is improved on its own schedule, and you never sleep in a construction site.
words.techContext: We used the strangler fig pattern to extract inventory from our Rails monolith over 18 months — each product category's inventory was migrated independently, and we kept the original Rails code as a fallback until each category proved stable.
words.exampleSentence: The strangler fig pattern let us migrate authentication to its own service while the monolith remained the backup — when the new auth service hit 99.99% reliability for a month, we removed the old code from the monolith.
words.etymology: Named by Martin Fowler in his 2004 essay 'Strangler Application' after the strangler fig tree (Ficus aurea), which germinates in the canopy of a host tree, grows roots around the trunk, and eventually replaces the host entirely — a natural metaphor for incremental system replacement.

words.shortDefinition: Drawing service boundaries around what the organization does — order management, inventory, billing — rather than technical layers.
words.simpleDefinition: Business capability decomposition means deciding where to draw service boundaries by asking 'what does this part of the business do?' rather than 'what technical layer does this code belong to?'. A business capability is a stable unit of value-producing function — inventory management, customer billing, shipment tracking. Services aligned to capabilities change when the business changes, not when a developer decides to refactor. This alignment is what makes microservices long-lived and maintainable.
words.longDefinition: Business capability decomposition is the primary decomposition strategy for microservices architecture. A business capability represents what the organization does to generate or support value: order fulfillment, inventory management, customer authentication, fraud detection, pricing calculation. These capabilities are stable — they change at the pace of business strategy, not at the pace of technical iteration. By drawing service boundaries around capabilities rather than around technical tiers (a database-access service, a validation service, a formatting service), you produce services that align with team ownership, change together for business reasons, and remain stable over time. Amazon's organizational model is the canonical example: each team owns a business capability end-to-end. Melvin Conway's observation (Conway's Law) predicts this outcome: organizations produce systems that mirror their communication structure, so if you want capability-aligned services, you need capability-aligned teams. The Inverse Conway Maneuver applies this constructively: design the team topology first, then let the system architecture follow.
words.connector: Think of business capability decomposition like organising a department store — you create a shoes department, a electronics department, a clothing department. Each serves a clear customer need. You don't create a 'cash register department' that spans all floors.
words.techContext: When we decomposed by business capability rather than technical layer, our team handoffs dropped dramatically — each team owned the full stack for their capability, so cross-team changes became rare.
words.exampleSentence: Business capability decomposition gave us services that matched our org chart: the pricing team owns the pricing service, the fulfillment team owns the fulfillment service — changes never cross team boundaries.
words.etymology: Compound of 'business capability' (enterprise architecture term for a stable unit of organizational function, formalized in TOGAF and Zachman frameworks) + 'decomposition' (Latin 'decomponere', to take apart). Applied to microservices decomposition by Chris Richardson in 'Microservices Patterns' (2018), drawing on Melvin Conway's 1968 organizational theory.

words.shortDefinition: A methodology of twelve operational and design principles for building portable, maintainable cloud-native services.
words.simpleDefinition: The Twelve-Factor App is a set of twelve best practices for building services that run well in the cloud. The factors cover topics like storing configuration in environment variables rather than code, treating logs as event streams, keeping development and production environments as similar as possible, and designing processes to start fast and shut down gracefully. Services that follow these factors are portable across cloud providers, easy to scale, and simple to operate.
words.longDefinition: The Twelve-Factor App methodology was articulated to document the patterns shared by well-operated cloud-native applications. The twelve factors are: (I) Codebase — one codebase per service in version control; (II) Dependencies — explicitly declare all dependencies, isolate them; (III) Config — store configuration in environment variables, never in code; (IV) Backing services — treat databases, queues, and caches as attached resources swappable by config; (V) Build, release, run — strictly separate the build, release, and execution stages; (VI) Processes — execute the service as stateless processes; (VII) Port binding — export services via port binding, not application server injection; (VIII) Concurrency — scale out via the process model; (IX) Disposability — maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown; (X) Dev/prod parity — keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible; (XI) Logs — treat logs as event streams, never manage log files; (XII) Admin processes — run admin/management tasks as one-off processes. In microservices, factors III (config), VI (stateless processes), IX (disposability), and X (dev/prod parity) are especially relevant — they directly enable independent deployability, container-based orchestration, and reliable CI/CD pipelines.
words.connector: Think of the Twelve-Factor App methodology like a building code for cloud services — not every rule feels urgent until you violate one and discover why it exists, like hardcoding a database URL that breaks every deployment.
words.techContext: Auditing our services against the twelve factors revealed that three services were reading config from checked-in files (Factor III violation) and two were writing logs to disk (Factor XI violation) — both caused painful production incidents.
words.exampleSentence: By following the twelve-factor principle of storing config in environment variables, we can deploy the same container image to dev, staging, and production — the environment determines the behavior, not the code.

codeExample.code:
import os

# Factor III: Config — read everything from environment variables
DB_URL       = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]    # not hardcoded
REDIS_URL    = os.environ["REDIS_URL"]       # not hardcoded
SECRET_KEY   = os.environ["SECRET_KEY"]      # never in source code
LOG_LEVEL    = os.environ.get("LOG_LEVEL", "INFO")

# Factor XI: Logs — write to stdout, not to files
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(
    stream=sys.stdout,   # the platform captures and routes log streams
    level=LOG_LEVEL,
    format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s'
)

# Factor IX: Disposability — handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown
import signal
def handle_sigterm(signum, frame):
    # finish in-flight requests, then exit cleanly
    server.shutdown()
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handle_sigterm)

words.etymology: Named for its enumeration of twelve numbered practices ('factors'). The methodology was developed and documented by engineers at Heroku, drawing on experience operating a large fleet of cloud applications. Published online as an open methodology.

words.shortDefinition: The observation that systems mirror the communication structures of the organizations that build them.
words.simpleDefinition: Conway's Law says that the shape of a software system will end up looking like the org chart of the team that built it. If three siloed teams build one system together, the system will have three subsystems with awkward interfaces matching the gaps in their communication. In microservices, this observation is used constructively: design the team topology you want, and the system architecture will follow naturally.
words.longDefinition: Conway's Law was stated by computer scientist Melvin Conway in 1968: 'Organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of those organizations.' The law is empirically observed, not mathematically proven, but decades of software history have confirmed it repeatedly. If a database team, a backend team, and a frontend team build a product together, you get a database layer, a backend layer, and a frontend layer — regardless of whether that layering makes architectural sense. In microservices, Conway's Law is used constructively via the Inverse Conway Maneuver: before designing the system, design the teams. If you want a services architecture aligned with business capabilities, organize teams around those capabilities. Amazon's two-pizza teams, Spotify's squad model, and Shopify's pods all apply this principle. Independent teams produce independently deployable services; tightly coupled teams produce tightly coupled services.
words.connector: Think of Conway's Law like the way a city's road network reflects its historical settlement patterns — paths form where people walked, roads follow paths, highways follow roads. The communication structure of the builders shapes the structure of what they build.
words.techContext: After recognizing Conway's Law, we restructured from functional teams (backend, frontend, QA) into product teams aligned to business capabilities — six months later our microservice boundaries finally matched the team boundaries.
words.exampleSentence: Conway's Law predicted our integration problems perfectly — our three-silo org produced a three-tier architecture, and every cross-cutting feature required coordinating all three teams.
words.etymology: Named after computer scientist Melvin Conway, who stated the observation in his 1967 paper 'How Do Committees Invent?' submitted to Harvard Business Review (and published in Datamation, April 1968). Fred Brooks popularized it in 'The Mythical Man-Month' (1975), calling it Conway's Law — a label Conway himself did not use.

words.shortDefinition: The anti-pattern of deploying multiple services that cannot be released independently due to tight coupling.
words.simpleDefinition: A distributed monolith is the worst of both worlds: you have all the operational complexity of microservices — multiple deployments, network calls, distributed tracing — but none of the benefits, because the services are so tightly coupled they still must be deployed together. Common causes are a shared database that multiple services read and write directly, synchronous call chains where every service depends on every other, or shared business logic libraries that couple release cycles.
words.longDefinition: Sam Newman coined the term 'distributed monolith' for a common anti-pattern: a system that structurally resembles microservices (multiple processes, multiple deployments, service-to-service HTTP calls) but which in practice cannot deploy any service without coordinating with the others. The team still has all the complexity of distributed systems — network failures, distributed tracing, multiple pipelines — without the benefits of independence. The most common cause is a shared database: when five services all read and write the same database schema, a schema change in Service A's table breaks Services B, C, D, and E. The team must coordinate and deploy all five simultaneously — exactly what microservices were supposed to eliminate. Other causes: synchronous call chains that create hard runtime dependencies, shared libraries containing domain logic that couples release schedules, and contracts so fine-grained that every feature change touches multiple services. The fix is not faster deployment tooling — it is redesigning the coupling at the architectural level.
words.connector: Think of a distributed monolith like a group of dancers who all have to move together even though they're standing in different corners of the stage — they're physically distributed but they're still performing the same synchronized routine.
words.techContext: We had nine microservices but still deployed them all together every Friday because our shared PostgreSQL schema meant any one service's migration could break the others — textbook distributed monolith.
words.exampleSentence: Our distributed monolith revealed itself the moment we tried to deploy the search service alone and discovered it would break because it read directly from the orders schema that the order service was also migrating.
words.etymology: Compound of 'distributed' (spread across multiple nodes or processes) + 'monolith' (a single indivisible unit). Coined by Sam Newman in 'Building Microservices' to name the anti-pattern of distributed deployment without distributed independence.
